# Apple Platform Design System: Accessibility

Self-contained. The skill's rules, then this topic, then anything it relies on from other skills.

## Skill rules

SwiftUI only. No UIKit unless explicitly required.

Baseline is iOS 27 / iPadOS 27 / macOS 27 Golden Gate, built with the Xcode 27 SDK. Code and design files both follow the 27 design language. There's no compatibility opt-out. Version numbers, dates, and what changed since 26 live only in [reference/platform-status.md](platform-status.md). Read it before quoting a version, before using an API marked (27) in a project that deploys to 26, and for any 26-era code or design file.

### Philosophy

Liquid Glass is a navigation-layer material. It floats above content. It does not touch content.

Three layers, in order:
1. Content (bottom): lists, media, text, cards. No glass.
2. Navigation (middle): toolbars, tab bars, sidebars, floating controls. Liquid Glass lives here.
3. Overlay (top): vibrancy, fills, and text rendered on glass surfaces.

If you're applying glass to content, you're doing it wrong. Cards are content. The API, the values, and the one system exception are in liquid-glass.md.

### Platform Visual Signature

A correct design is immediately recognizable as Apple-made. If it reads as a web app or as Android, it's wrong. Check this on nearly every task.

**What makes it immediately look like iOS:**
- Tab bar sits at the bottom of the screen with glass treatment, floating above content
- Content scrolls behind both the status bar at top and the tab bar at bottom (edge-to-edge)
- Navigation is push-based: screens slide left/right. Back button in the upper-left.
- Large title at the top of a navigation stack collapses as the user scrolls
- Partial-height sheets are inset from the screen edges, float with rounded corners and a glass background, and turn more opaque when expanded to full height
- SF Pro font throughout. No third-party fonts unless deliberately part of a brand decision.
- SF Symbols for all iconography. No custom icon libraries.
- Semantic colors. The background shifts automatically between light and dark.

**What makes it immediately look like macOS:**
- Standard window chrome (traffic light buttons top-left, window title centered or leading)
- Sidebar on the left with icon + label navigation, running edge-to-edge (top, bottom, and side of the window). Part of the window, not an inset floating panel. Icons take the accent color. In an inactive window, icons and text dim.
- Toolbar at the top with glass controls on the system's uniform toolbar treatment, the same in every app
- Window shape and corner radius are the system's. Contained elements are concentric with it. An app doesn't design its own window radius.
- Menus carry icons only where they clarify. Most menu items are text only.

**Wrong if:**
- Tab bar is at the top (that's web or Android)
- Navigation bar has a solid opaque background (content should extend behind it)
- Colors are hardcoded instead of semantic (system semantic colors, or the project's own semantic tokens)
- Icons are not SF Symbols
- Text fields, buttons, or lists look like generic HTML form controls
- There is no glass treatment on the navigation layer
- A partial-height sheet is flush to the screen edges with no inset rounding
- Safe areas are ignored (content or interactive elements under the status bar or in the home indicator zone)
- A Mac sidebar is drawn as an inset floating card, or a Mac toolbar's transparency is hand-tuned per screen (both are the 26 look)

## Topic

The system handles a lot automatically. Don't fight it.

### What the system adapts

- **Reduce Transparency**: glass gets frostier and more opaque. Standard components and `.glassEffect()` fall back on their own.
- **Increase Contrast**: stark colors, borders, and higher-contrast backgrounds on glass elements.
- **Reduce Motion**: Liquid Glass tones down its elastic interactions. Cut or minimize your own animations and use opacity transitions.
- **Liquid Glass slider** (Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass): more clear to more tint. Unavailable while Reduce Transparency or Increase Contrast is on, so it never combines with them.

Test with each one on. Test custom glass at both ends of the slider. Reduce Transparency is the one that gets missed: the UI still has to show hierarchy and depth with no translucency.

### What the app owns

System glass needs no code for any of that. Don't swap `.glassEffect()` for `.identity` when Reduce Transparency is on. That removes the background the system would have made opaque and leaves the label floating on content.

The environment values are for translucency and motion you draw yourself: custom materials, shader effects, gradients over media, hand-built transitions.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceTransparency) private var reduceTransparency
@Environment(\.colorSchemeContrast) private var contrast

var scrim: some ShapeStyle {
    reduceTransparency ? AnyShapeStyle(.background) : AnyShapeStyle(.ultraThinMaterial)
}
```

`accessibilityReduceMotion` is in `motion-interaction.md`.

Every custom color needs four variants: light, dark, and an increased-contrast version of each. System colors already have them.

### Requirements

Dynamic Type: all text scales. No fixed-height containers that truncate text. Custom sizes scale through `@ScaledMetric` or a text-style-relative font (`color-typography.md`).

VoiceOver: every interactive element has an accessibility label. Icon-only glass buttons and toolbar items get explicit ones.

Touch targets: 44x44pt minimum on iOS and iPadOS. Always. Don't shrink tap areas to fit a tighter glass composition. The HIG allows 28x28 as a floor. I don't go below 44. On macOS the HIG default is 28x28.

Contrast ratios (WCAG AA, the values Accessibility Inspector checks):
- Text up to 17pt: 4.5:1
- Text 18pt and larger, or bold at any size: 3:1
- Interactive elements against adjacent colors: 3:1

Measure these **with the glass applied**, against the real content behind it, not against the glass fill color. The material can cut contrast a lot depending on what's under it. Test the worst-case background, at the clear end of the Liquid Glass slider, in both appearances.
